text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Turpel-Lafond v. British Columbia,

2019 BCSC 51

Date: 20190117

Docket:
S171076

Registry: Victoria

Between:

Mary
Ellen Turpel-Lafond

Plaintiff

And

Her
Majesty the Queen in Right of the Province of British Columbia and the
Legislative Assembly of British Columbia

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Chief Justice Hinkson

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

J.J.
Arvay, Q.C.

A. Beddoes

Counsel for Her Majesty the Queen in
Right of the Province of British Columbia:

D.
P.J. Lawton, Q.C.

A.
Bookman

Counsel for the Legislative Assembly of
British Columbia

G.
Plant, Q.C.

S.
Ramdin

Place and Date of Hearing:

Victoria,
B.C.

October
2 and 3, 2018

Place and Date of Judgment:

Victoria,
B.C.

January
17, 2019

I.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

In 2006, the plaintiff, Ms. Turpel-Lafond,
was a judge of the Provincial Court of Saskatchewan, and the administrative
judge for Saskatoon. She then became the first Representative for Children and
Youth (“RCY”) in British Columbia. The RCY position replaced the Acting Child
and Youth Officer (“CYO”) as the advocate for children and youth in the
province. Correspondingly, the
Representative for Children and Youth Act
,
S.B.C. 2006, c. 29 [
RCY Ac
t], replaced the
Office for Children
and Youth Act
, S.B.C. 2002, c. 50 [
CYO Act
]. To facilitate this
transition, in addition to being appointed as RCY in November 2006 for a five-year
term, Ms. Turpel-Lafond was appointed as CYO in December 2006 for an
effective period of January 1, 2007, to March 31, 2007. In the result, the
province of British Columbia entered into two written agreements with Ms. Turpel-Lafond
concerning these appointments.

[
2
]

Both defendants are defined in
s. 29
of the

Interpretation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 238
. The government of British
Columbia is defined as “Her Majesty in right of British Columbia” and the
“Legislative Assembly” is defined as “the Legislative Assembly of British
Columbia constituted under the
Constitution Act
.” “Legislature” is
constituted in accordance with s. 17 of the
Constitution Act
and is
defined at s. 29 of the
Interpretation Act
as “the Lieutenant
Governor acting by and with the advice and consent of the Legislative
Assembly.” At all material times, the Legislative Assembly was the legislative
branch of the B.C. government.

[
3
]

The Legislative Assembly of British Columbia has
the authority to appoint an RCY under the provisions of the
RCY Act
.
Once appointed, the RCY is an officer of the legislature. The
OCY Act
,
by contrast, provided that the CYO was appointed by the Lieutenant Governor in
Council or the Attorney General.

[
4
]

Under s. 3 of the
RCY Act
, the RCY
is statutorily entitled to certain compensation. By contrast, s. 2 of the
OCY
Act
provided that compensation was to be determined by contract. In the
plaintiff’s case, given these unique circumstances, her CYO appointment letter provided
that her only remuneration as CYO would be the salary and benefits that she would
receive as RCY.

[
5
]

The plaintiff took her oath of office as the RCY
on December 4, 2006. She served two consecutive terms with her second term of
office commencing on November 27, 2011, and concluding on or about November 27,
2016. A third term is not permitted pursuant to
s. 2(4)
of the
RCY Act
.

[
6
]

During the application and interview process for
the RCY position in 2006, Ms. Turpel-Lafond contends that she engaged in
negotiations with the Deputy Clerk of the Legislative Assembly and Clerk of
Committees (“Deputy Clerk”) due to concerns about the compensation and benefits
she would receive if appointed as RCY.

[
7
]

It is this negotiation and alleged eventual agreement
that underlies the plaintiff’s claim against the defendants, the Legislative
Assembly of British Columbia (the “Legislative Assembly”) and the government of
the province of British Columbia (the “Government”). She contends that both
defendants entered into a verbal contract with her setting out certain
conditions that would govern her remuneration as RCY and CYO if she were
appointed. She says that neither defendant fulfilled these conditions and that
they therefore breached their verbal agreements. She further alleges that both
defendants negligently misrepresented to her that they would provide her with
enhanced pension entitlement and reimbursement for moving expenses. She seeks
damages as a result.

[
8
]

The present applications were filed by each
defendant seeking to strike the plaintiff’s amended notice of civil claim (the
“amended notice”) under Rules 9-5 and 9-6 of the

Supreme Court Civil Rules
,
B.C. Reg. 168/2009 [
Rules
].

[
9
]

The Legislative Assembly seeks an order
dismissing the plaintiff’s claim or staying the proceedings against it due to
lack of jurisdiction, arguing that the amended notice is unnecessary and
frivolous under Rule 9-5(1)(b), an abuse of process under Rule 9-5(1)(d), and
has no reasonable prospect of success pursuant to Rule 9-6(4).

[
10
]

The orders sought by the Government include:

1.         An order that the plaintiff’s amended
notice of civil claim against the Government be struck out pursuant to Rule
9-5(1)(a) of the
Rules

as disclosing no reasonable claim;

2.         In the alternative, an order that the plaintiff’s
amended notice of civil claim against the Government be struck out pursuant to
Rule 9-5(1)(b) as being unnecessary and frivolous; and

3.         In the alternative, an order that the plaintiff’s
claim against the Government be dismissed on the basis that the claim has no
reasonable prospect of success pursuant to Rule 9-6(5).

II.

BASIS OF THE PLAINTIFF’S CLAIM

[
11
]

In her amended notice of civil claim, the
plaintiff alleges that:

a)

In or around August 2006, she responded to an advertisement for the
position of British Columbia’s RCY. The following month she was contacted by
the Deputy Clerk and invited to attend an in-person interview for the position.

b)

In the ensuing months, discussions regarding the plaintiff’s
application for the position occurred through a series of meetings, emails, and
telephone calls with the Deputy Clerk and other representatives of either the Government
or the Legislative Assembly. These communications included plans for her
interview, and the terms upon which she would be appointed.

c)

She entered into a verbal contract with the defendants whereby she
would serve, initially as both the CYO for the province of British Columbia and
RCY, and later as just the RCY on terms that included:

i.

1.5 years pension entitlement for each year of service;

ii.

reimbursement for all expenses associated with her relocation from
Saskatchewan to Victoria, British Columbia;

iii.

reimbursement for all house sale and purchase costs, including
transaction costs;

iv.

reimbursement for short-term rental costs in Victoria, British
Columbia until permanently settled there; and

v.

reimbursement for all expenses associated with the relocation of
herself and her family back to Saskatchewan upon the completion of her
engagement.

d)

The Attorney General of British Columbia assured her that whatever
arrangements were required in order for her to accept the appointment as RCY would
be made. She deposed that on

November 21, 2006, the Deputy Clerk
informed her that following considerable review of her pension requirements by
various individuals, including the Attorney General, approval had been given
for her pension formula to be amended such that she would receive 1.5 years of
pension entitlement for each year of service.

e)

She accepted the appointment and, as a condition of the appointment,
sought a leave of absence from her position as a judge. As a condition of
obtaining her leave of absence, she was required to waive her right to make
contributions to the Saskatchewan judges’ pension during the leave of absence.

f)

The Deputy Clerk provided her with a

letter dated December
29, 2006, that confirmed that he was “… recommending an amendment to the
Representative
for Children and Youth Act
to provide the Representative for Children and
Youth with a pension entitlement of 1.5 years of credit for each year served to
be consistent with the other Statutory Officers”.

III.        POSITIONS OF THE
PARTIES

[
12
]

The Legislative Assembly’s argument that the plaintiff’s
claim should be struck rests upon the doctrine of parliamentary privilege. According
to the Legislative Assembly, the RCY’s remuneration scheme is within a
recognized category of parliamentary privilege to appoint and manage its staff
that have a role in holding the government to account. The Legislative Assembly
contends that allowing the plaintiff’s claim to go to trial would require the
court to inquire into the Legislative Assembly’s internal proceedings and its
management of the plaintiff and that such judicial interference would undermine
the autonomy of the Legislative Assembly and the ability of its officers to
conduct their business. The Legislative Assembly further contends that the plaintiff’s
remuneration as the RCY falls squarely within the scope of parliamentary
privilege and therefore is the exclusive jurisdiction of the legislature.

[
13
]

Given the court’s alleged lack of jurisdiction
over the claim, the Legislative Assembly argues that the plaintiff’s claim is
unnecessary or vexatious, without foundation, would serve no useful purpose,
and is bound to fail, as the pleadings do not provide a
bona fide
triable
issue. Accordingly, the Legislative Assembly argues that the plaintiff’s claim
should be dismissed or stayed.

[
14
]

The plaintiff, in response to the Legislative
Assembly, argues that her claims do not impugn any acts of the Legislative
Assembly that are sufficiently connected to its core legislative and
deliberative functions to bring it within the scope of parliamentary privilege.
Adjudicating the plaintiff’s claims would not interfere with its ability to do
its legislative work. While issues relating to appointment and removal of
officers of the legislature may be within the scope of parliamentary privilege,
whether or not the legislature has complied with contractual terms of service
can properly be adjudicated as such a claim is, in essence, one based in
private law. In the alternative, the plaintiff suggests that the issue of
parliamentary privilege and its applicability to her claim is more
appropriately determined at trial and not struck at this stage of the
proceedings.

[
15
]

The Government contends that if parliamentary
privilege applies, the entire claim against both defendants must be dismissed
because the Government cannot be held accountable for anything done within the
scope of parliamentary privilege. Even if the plaintiff has a justiciable
claim, however, the Government says that it is not a proper party, as the RCY
is not appointed by, nor employed, by the Government. In the further
alternative, the Government argues that the plain wording of the agreement
precludes a claim against it because the plaintiff’s pension and other benefits
were legislated pursuant to
s. 3(2)
of the
RCY Act
. Any further
oral agreement dealing with remuneration and benefits therefore would be
contrary to the
RCY Act
and unenforceable. Third, it says that it cannot
be vicariously liable for representations made by the Deputy Clerk, a permanent
officer of the Legislative Assembly. Finally, it argues that the separation of
powers dictates that it cannot be the plaintiff’s common employer. Therefore, the
Government asks this Court to strike the plaintiff’s pleadings as unnecessary and
disclosing no reasonable claim against it as a matter of law, and because the
plaintiff has no reasonable prospect of success.

[
16
]

In response to the Government, the plaintiff
argues her claims should not be dismissed at this stage. First, even if
parliamentary privilege applies with respect to her claims against the Legislative
Assembly, parliamentary privilege cannot shield the Government. Further, while
the
RCY Act
sets out some aspects of the plaintiff’s entitlements, she
says it is not exhaustive and could be supplemented by agreement. As the Government
was responsible for paying the plaintiff both as RCY and CYO, the Government
was the party responsible for ensuring she would be paid based on her contract.
She contends that her claim should not be struck on the basis that any
agreement would be unenforceable or that the Government is not the proper
defendant to the plaintiff’s claim.

[
17
]

The plaintiff further argues that much of her
evidence is uncontroverted. The Government has not explained why the Deputy
Clerk did not act as its agent nor provided any evidence to contradict that of
the plaintiff. Nor did the Government adduce evidence to contradict her claim
that the Attorney General, and other government employees, participated in negotiating
and finalizing her contractual entitlements. These claims, therefore, must be
determined at trial.

[
18
]

Finally, and in the alternative, the plaintiff
argues that the Legislative Assembly and the Government are jointly liable as
common employers, a question of fact that cannot be determined on the
evidentiary record on this application and a matter properly determined at
trial.

IV.       ISSUES

[
19
]

The issues that must be determined in these
applications are:

a)

whether the court lacks jurisdiction to adjudicate the plaintiff’s
claim pursuant to the doctrine of parliamentary privilege;

b)

if not, whether the plaintiff’s amended notice should nevertheless
be struck on the basis that it:

(1)

discloses no reasonable claim under Rule
9-5(1)(a);

(2)

is unnecessary and frivolous under Rule
9-5(1)(b); or

(3)

has no reasonable prospect of success under Rule
9-6(4).

V.        DISCUSSION

1.         Legal Framework to Strike Claims

[
20
]

Rule 9-5 of the
Rules
provides, in part,
that:

9-5
(1)
At any
stage of a proceeding, the court may order to be struck out or amended the
whole or any part of a pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)

it discloses no reasonable claim
or defence, as the case may be,

(b) it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

…

(d) it is otherwise
an abuse of the process of the court

and the court may pronounce judgment or
order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the
application to be paid as special costs.

[
21
]

On an application to strike under Rule
9-5(1)(a), Chief Justice McLachlin commented in
R. v. Imperial Tobacco
Canada Ltd.
,
2011 SCC 42
, that:

[17]      …A claim will only be struck if it
is plain and obvious, assuming the facts pleaded to be true, that the pleading
discloses no reasonable cause of action:
Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse
,

2003 SCC 69 (CanLII)
, [2003] 3 S.C.R. 263, at para.
15
;
Hunt v. Carey
Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, at p. 980. Another
way of putting the test is that the claim has no reasonable prospect of
success.

[
22
]

Pursuant to Rule 9-5(2), no evidence is
admissible on an application to strike under subrule (1)(a). The analysis is
focussed on the pleadings alone and proceeds on the basis that the facts
pleaded are true, unless they are “manifestly incapable of being proven”:
Imperial
Tobacco
at para. 22. As Madam Justice Fisher observed in
Willow v. Chong
,

2013 BCSC 1083
at para.
19
, this “does not mean that allegations based on
assumption and speculation must be taken as true”. A judge also cannot consider
what evidence adduced in the future might or might not prove:
Imperial
Tobacco
at para. 23.

[
23
]

With respect to an application under Rule 9-5(1)(b)
that deals with pleadings that are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or
vexatious, Mr. Justice Cullen, as he then was, summarized the law in
Woolsey
v. Dawson Creek (City)
,
2011 BCSC 751
, as follows:

28        In a similar vein, in
Wayneroy
Holdings Ltd. v. Sideen
,
2002 BCSC 1510 (CanLII)
, [2002] B.C.J. No. 2472 (B.C. S.C.), Romilly
J. quoted from the judgment in
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v.
Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160 (B.C. S.C. [In
Chambers]) as follows:

The authorities
provide little guidance as to what constitutes pleadings that are
"unnecessary", "scandalous", "frivolous" or
"embarrassing". However some principles do emerge.

Irrelevancy and
embarrassment are both established when pleadings are so confusing that it is
difficult to understand what is being pleaded ... An "embarrassing"
and "scandalous" pleading is one that is so irrelevant that it will
involve the parties in useless expense and will prejudice the [pursuit] of the
action by involving them in a dispute apart from the issues ... An allegation
which is scandalous will not be struck if it is relevant to the proceedings. It
will only be struck if irrelevant as well as scandalous ...
A pleading is
"unnecessary" or "vexatious" if it does not go to
establishing the plaintiff's cause of action or does not advance any claim
known in law
... A pleading that is superfluous will not be struck out if
it is not necessarily unnecessary or otherwise objectionable ...

[Emphasis added.]

[
24
]

Another basis upon which to strike pleadings is
when the matter is considered an “abuse of process” under Rule 9-5(1)(d). In
Sidhu
v. Sidhu
,
2008 BCSC 324
, Madam Justice Bruce summarized this basis as
follows at para. 24:

Abuse of process is a flexible doctrine and
the categories of abuse are not closed. In
Babavic v. Babowech
,
[1993]
B.C.J. No. 1802 (S.C.) (QL)
, the circumstances in which the court may
exercise its discretion to strike a pleading for abuse of process are described
by Baker J. at para. 18:

The categories of abuse
of process are open. Abuse of process may be found where proceedings involve a
deception on the court or constitute a mere sham; where the process of the
court is not being fairly or honestly used, or is employed for some ulterior or
improper purpose;
proceedings which are without foundation or serve no
useful purpose
and multiple or successive proceedings which cause or are
likely to cause vexation or oppression.

[Emphasis added.]

[
25
]

In
Imperial Tobacco
at para. 21
,
McLachlin
C.J.C. cautioned that a motion to strike “must be used with care” and that the
court’s approach must “be generous and err on the side of permitting a novel
but arguable claim to proceed to trial.”

[
26
]

In
Moses v. Lower Nicola Indian Band
,

2015 BCCA 61
, Madam Justice Newbury stated at para. 45 that there is a
high onus to strike pleadings under Rule 9-5.

[
27
]

Under Rule 9-6, a pleading can be dismissed if
insufficient material facts are plead to support it. That rule provides, in
part:

(4)

In an action, an answering party
may, after serving a responding pleading on a claiming party, apply under this
rule for judgment dismissing all or part of a claim in the claiming party's
originating pleading.

(5)

On hearing an application under
subrule (2) or (4), the court,

(a)

if satisfied that there is no genuine issue for trial with respect
to a claim or defence, must pronounce judgment or dismiss the claim
accordingly,

(b)

if satisfied that the only genuine issue is the amount to which the
claiming party is entitled, may order a trial of that issue or pronounce
judgment with a reference or an accounting to determine the amount,

(c)
if satisfied that the only
genuine issue is a question of law, may determine the question and pronounce
judgment accordingly, and

(d)
may make any other order it
considers will further the object of these
Supreme Court Civil Rules
.

[
28
]

As with Rule 9-5, the defendant bears a heavy
burden to succeed under Rule 9-6. The defendant must demonstrate that there is
no “genuine issue of material fact requiring trial”:
McLean v. Law Society
of British Columbia
,
2016 BCCA 368
at para.
36
;
Canada (Attorney
General) v. Lameman
,
2008 SCC 14
at para.
11
. If the defendant meets
this burden, the plaintiff must either refute the defendant’s evidence or risk
summary dismissal:
Lameman
at para.
11
.

[
29
]

Unlike Rule 9-5, which is an attack on the
pleadings on the basis that the claim or defence cannot succeed as a matter of
law, Rule 9-6 is concerned with whether the claim is factually without merit:
see
McLean
at para. 37. As explained by Mr. Justice Thackray in

Skybridge Investments Ltd. v. Metro Motors Ltd.
,
2006 BCCA 500
,
at
paras.
11–12
:

11        If insufficient material facts
have been pleaded to support every element of a cause of action, then beyond a
doubt that cause of action is bound to fail and a defendant bringing an
application pursuant to Rule 18(6) will have met the onus to negative the
existence of a bona fide triable issue.

12        If sufficient material facts have
been pleaded to support every element of a cause of action, but one or more of
those pleaded material facts are contested, then the judge ruling on a Rule
18(6) application is not to weigh the evidence to determine the issue of fact
for the purpose of the application. The judge's function is limited to a determination
as to whether a bona fide triable issue arises on the material before the court
in the context of the applicable law. If a judge ruling on a Rule 18(6)
application must assess and weigh the evidence to arrive at a summary judgment,
the "plain and obvious" or "beyond a doubt" test has not
been met.

[
30
]

The determination must be based on the pleadings
and the evidence before the court, not on what might be proved if the claim is
permitted to proceed:
Lameman
at para.
19
.

[
31
]

Under this rule, an action may be dismissed on
the basis that it is “bound to lose”, or, that there is no
bona fide
triable
issue:
Pitt v. Holt
,
2007 BCSC 1555
. In
Skybridge
, Thackray J.A.
heard an application under Rule 18-6 (now Rule 9-6) and summarized the
procedure to be followed as such:

10        A judge hearing an application
pursuant to Rule 18(6) must: examine the pleaded facts to determine which
causes of action they may support; identify the essential elements required to
be proved at trial in order to succeed on each cause of action; and determine
if sufficient material facts have been pleaded to support each element of a
given cause of action.

2.         Analysis

A.        Does the Doctrine
of Parliamentary Privilege Apply?

[
32
]

The first basis on which the defendants contend
the plaintiff’s claims should be struck relies on the doctrine of parliamentary
privilege. This doctrine is concerned with whether the court has jurisdiction
to adjudicate the plaintiff’s claim. If privilege applies, the claim would
properly be struck, as the legislature would have exclusive jurisdiction over
it.

i.          Legal Principles

[
33
]

In
New Brunswick Broadcasting Co. v. Nova
Scotia (Speaker of the House of Assembly),

1993 CanLII 153 (SCC)
, [1993] 1 S.C.R. 319 at 378,
Madam Justice McLachlin, as she then was, discussed parliamentary privilege:

I turn first, to the historical tradition of
parliamentary privileges. "Privilege” in this context denotes the legal
exemption from some duty, burden, attendance or liability to which others are
subject. It has long been accepted that in order to perform their functions,
legislative bodies require certain privileges relating to the conduct of their
business. It has also long been accepted that these privileges must be held
absolutely and constitutionally if they are to be effective; the legislative
branch of our government must enjoy a certain autonomy which even the Crown and
the courts cannot touch.

[
34
]

At page 389 she added the following:

…Our democratic government consists of
several branches: the Crown, as represented by the Governor General and the
provincial counterparts of that office; the legislative body; the executive;
and the courts. It is fundamental to the working of government as a whole that
all these parts play their proper role. It is equally fundamental that no one
of them overstep its bounds, that each show proper deference for the legitimate
sphere of activity of the other.

[
35
]

In British Columbia, the
Legislative Assembly
Privilege Act,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 259, has codified the individual and
collective privileges that exist for committees and members of the Legislative
Assembly at s. 1(1):

Those are the privileges held and exercised
by the Commons House of Parliament of the United Kingdom and its committees and
members on February 14, 1871, so far as not inconsistent with the
Constitution
Act
, whether held or exercised by custom, statute or otherwise.

[
36
]

When considering a claim of parliamentary
privilege, courts are required to first determine whether the activity is
within an already recognized category of parliamentary privilege:
Canada (House
of Commons) v. Vaid
,
2005 SCC 30
at para.
39
[
Vaid
]. In
Vaid
,

Mr. Justice Binnie summarized the existing categories of privilege at para. 29
as follows:

[29]      …

10.       “Categories”
include freedom of speech; control by the Houses of Parliament over “debates or
proceedings in Parliament” (as guaranteed by the Bill of Rights of 1689)
including day-to-day procedure in the House, for example the practice of the
Ontario legislature to start the day’s sitting with the Lord’s Prayer; the
power to exclude strangers from proceedings; disciplinary authority over
members; and non-members who interfere with the discharge of parliamentary
duties, including immunity of members from subpoenas during a parliamentary
session. Such general categories have historically been considered to be
justified by the exigencies of parliamentary work.

[Citations
omitted.]

[
37
]

If the privilege applies, the courts have no
jurisdiction to consider the matters falling within it or whether an exercise
of privilege in a given case is necessary or appropriate:
Vaid
at para.
29
;
Chagnon

v. Syndicat de la fonction publique et
parapublique du Québec
,
2018 SCC 39
at para.
25

[
Chagnon
]. In other words, specific exercises of privilege within
categories are not reviewable:
Vaid
at para.
29
;
New Brunswick
Broadcasting
at 343. That said, a court may consider whether the category
remains necessary to the independent functioning of the legislature:
Chagnon

at para.
31
;
Vaid

at para.
29
(6);
New Brunswick
Broadcasting
at 387.

[
38
]

The Supreme Court of Canada has recently
reviewed the foundation for and applicability of parliamentary privilege in
Chagnon
.
Madam Justice Karakatsanis, for the majority, summarized as follows at paras. 18–19:

[18]      Legislative
assemblies in Canada, including provincial legislative assemblies, received
"certain very moderate [parliamentary] privileges" through the common
law as an inherent and necessary component of their legislative function, and
by virtue of the preamble of the
Constitution Act, 1867
(
New
Brunswick Broadcasting Co. v. Nova Scotia (Speaker of the House of Assembly)
,

1993 CanLII 153 (SCC)
, [1993] 1 S.C.R. 319, at p. 377, citing R. M. Dawson,
The Government of
Canada
(5th ed. 1970), at p. 338; see also
New Brunswick
Broadcasting
, at pp. 345 and 374-81;
Canada (House of Commons) v.
Vaid
,
2005 SCC 30
; [2005] 1 S.C.R. 667, at para. 29(3); J. P. J.
Maingot,
Parliamentary Immunity in Canada
(2016), at pp. 13 and
19).

[19]      Parliamentary
privilege is defined as "the sum of the privileges, immunities and powers
enjoyed by the Senate, the House of Commons and provincial legislative
assemblies, and by each member individually, without which they could not
discharge their functions" (
Vaid
, at para.
29
(2)). These
privileges, immunities, and powers exceed those afforded to the general
population (
Erskine May's Treatise on The Law, Privileges, Proceedings and
Usage of Parliament
(24th ed. 2011), by M. Jack, at p. 203).
Therefore, parliamentary privilege "is an exemption from some duty,
burden, attendance or liability to which others are subject" (Maingot, at
p. 13). Decisions falling within the scope of parliamentary privilege
cannot be reviewed by an external body, including a court (
Stockdale v.
Hansard

(1839), 9 Ad. & E. 1, 112 E.R. 1112 (Q.B.), at p. 1168
;
New
Brunswick Broadcasting
, at pp. 350 and 382-84;
Vaid
, at para.
29
(9)).

[
39
]

At para. 21, Karakatsanis J. adopted the
justification for legislative privileges articulated by the Supreme Court of
the United States in
Gravel v. United States
, 408 U.S. 606 (1972), at
616,
as allowing legislative bodies to fearlessly hold
the executive branch of government to account, thus helping to preserve the
separation and balance of power between the different branches of government
.

[
40
]

Karakatsanis J. explained at paras. 23–24:

[23]      In Canada,
parliamentary privilege is grounded in the preamble of the
Constitution Act,
1867
, which provides Canada with "a Constitution similar in Principle
to that of the United Kingdom". It is an inherent and necessary component
of the Westminster model of parliamentary democracy. As in the U.K., the
inherent privileges of Canadian legislative bodies are a means to preserve
their independence and promote the workings of representative democracy. It is
meant to enable the legislative branch and its members to proceed fearlessly
and without interference in discharging their constitutional role, that is,
enacting legislation and acting as a check on executive power (
New Brunswick
Broadcasting
, at p. 354;
Vaid
, at paras.
21 and 41
). It
guarantees "an independent space for the citizens' representatives to
carry out their parliamentary functions; the freedom to debate and decide what
laws should govern, and the unfettered ability to hold the executive branch of
the State to account" (S. R. Chaplin, "
House of Commons v. Vaid
:
Parliamentary Privilege and the Constitutional Imperative of the Independence
of Parliament" (2009), 2
J.P.P.L.
153, at p. 154).

[24]      When
tethered to its purposes, parliamentary privilege is an important part of the
public law of Canada (see
Vaid
, at para.
29
(3)). The insulation
from external review that privilege provides is a key component of our
constitutional structure and the law that governs it. Judicial review of the
exercise of parliamentary privilege, even for
Charter
compliance, would
effectively nullify the necessary immunity this doctrine is meant to afford the
legislature (
New Brunswick Broadcasting
, at pp. 350 and 382-84;
Vaid
,
at para.
29
(9)). However, while legislative assemblies are not accountable
to the courts for the ways in which they exercise their parliamentary
privileges, they remain accountable to the electorate (Chaplin, at p. 164).

[
41
]

While a court cannot consider specific exercises
of privilege within categories, a court may inquire into the existence and
scope of parliamentary privileges:

Vaid

at para.
29
;
Chagnon

at
para.
110
. In doing so, courts apply a test of necessity. In
Chagnon

at
paras.
29–30
, Karakatsanis J. summarized the test as follows:

[29]      In order
to fall within the scope of parliamentary privilege, the matter at issue must
meet the necessity test:
it must be "so closely and directly connected
with the fulfilment by the assembly or its members of their functions as a
legislative and deliberative body ... that outside interference would undermine
the level of autonomy required to enable the assembly and its members to do
their work with dignity and efficiency"
(
Vaid
, at para.
46
).

[30]      The
necessity test thus demands that the sphere of activity over which
parliamentary privilege is claimed be more than merely
connected
to the
legislative assembly's functions. The
immunity
that is sought from the
application of ordinary law must also be necessary to the assembly's
constitutional role. In other words, "[i]f a sphere of the legislative
body's activity could be left to be dealt with under the ordinary law of the
land without interfering with the assembly's ability to fulfil its
constitutional functions, then immunity would be unnecessary and the claimed
privilege would not exist" (
Vaid
, at para.
29
(5)).

[Underlining added.]

[
42
]

The party seeking to rely on the immunity from
external review bears the burden of establishing that it is “necessary” in
light of the purposes of parliamentary privilege:
Chagnon

at para.
32
.
Considerable deference is granted to the legislative body’s view regarding the
scope of the privilege that is necessary, but courts must ensure that the claim
of privilege does not “immunize from the ordinary law the consequences of
conduct by Parliament or its officers and employees that exceeds the necessary
scope of the categories of privilege”:
Chagnon

at para.
32
;
Vaid

at paras.
29, 40
. As Karakatsanis J. explained in
Chagnon
at paras.
25
and 27
:

[25]      Yet, while
the independence of the legislature is a necessary aspect of our constitutional
structure and is wholly part of our law, so are its limits. The inherent nature
of parliamentary privilege means that its existence and scope
must be
strictly anchored to its rationale
. Notably, it creates a sphere of
decision-making immune from judicial oversight for compliance with the
Charter
.
It may also impede persons who are not members of the legislature from
accessing recourses available under ordinary law (
Vaid
, at para.
30
).
As this Court explained in
Vaid
, "[c]ourts are apt to look more
closely at cases in which claims to privilege have an impact on persons outside
the legislative assembly than at those which involve matters entirely internal
to the legislature".

…

[27]
Thus, in Canada, the scope of parliamentary
privilege is delimited by the purposes it serves (see e.g.
Vaid
,

at paras.
41-46
). It inheres to the nature and functions of legislative
assemblies as a separate branch of government.
The reach of inherent
privilege extends only so far as is "necessary to protect legislators in
the discharge of their legislative and deliberative functions, and the
legislative assembly's work in holding the government to account for the
conduct of the country's business
" (
Vaid
,
at para.
41
; see also
New Brunswick Broadcasting
,
at pp. 381-85). Otherwise, it would unjustifiably trump other parts of the
Constitution.

[Emphasis added.]

ii.         Application of the Legal
Principles

[
43
]

The Legislative Assembly argues that inquiring
into the remuneration and benefits of an officer of the Legislative Assembly
falls squarely within a recognized category of parliamentary privilege. As a
result, the Legislative Assembly contends this Court is precluded from delving
into plaintiff’s claim on jurisdictional grounds. Specifically, the Legislative
Assembly contends that the claim falls within its privilege “to administer its
own affairs within the precincts, and appointing and managing its staff that
have a nexus with its legislative and deliberative functions or its role in
holding the government to account”, citing Joseph P. Maingot,
Parliamentary
Immunity in Canada
(Toronto: LexisNexis, 2016) at 167. This privilege
applies because the plaintiff’s role as RCY was to hold the government to
account with respect to children and youth in the province.

[
44
]

The Government agrees with the Legislative
Assembly. It argues that the doctrine of parliamentary privilege is dispositive
because if it applies, the claim is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the
legislature and the court is precluded from considering it, even as against the
Government.

[
45
]

In
Thompson v. McLean
,
1998 CanLII 14740 (ON CTGD)
, [1998] O.J. No. 2070
(C.J. (Gen. Div.)), [
Thompson
] a decision relied upon by the Government,
Mr. Justice Campbell dealt with an application to strike a claim
on a number of
grounds, including parliamentary privilege. In Ms. Thompson’s claim
for wrongful dismissal, she said that
her employment was
terminated after she alleged that the former Speaker of the Legislative
Assembly of the Province of Ontario sexually harassed her. Campbell J. declined
to strike out her claim as he concluded that whether parliamentary privilege
applied was better determined at trial. However, at para. 69 he commented
that:

The election of a Speaker to his office and
the decision to jettison a Speaker are not administrative nor personnel
decisions of the Office. They are political decisions made by members of the
Legislative Assembly. I
t is not for
the Court to inquire into the political decision, whether a Speaker should
continue in office.

[
46
]

As in this case, the claim in
Thompson

involved an officer of the Legislative Assembly. Unlike this case, however, the
plaintiff’s allegations in
Thompson
had to do with whether or not the
legislative officer could continue in his role as Speaker, not the remuneration
or benefits received in that role.

[
47
]

Further, neither defendant has asserted that Ms. Turpel-Lafond’s
right to remuneration for the fulfillment of her duties could be avoided on the
basis that she did not fulfill her duties, and she makes no allegation of
wrongful dismissal.

[
48
]

In support of its position, the Legislative
Assembly relies primarily on
Marin v. Office of the Ombudsman
,
2017 ONSC
1687
[
Marin
], where the plaintiff had been appointed the Ombudsman of
Ontario and brought a claim for damages for, amongst other things, wrongful
dismissal based on an alleged breach of an indefinite employment contract,
reimbursement of office expenses, and damages for negligent misrepresentation.
There, the Legislative Assembly of Ontario sought to dismiss or stay the claim on
the basis of parliamentary privilege. In allowing the Legislative Assembly’s
motion and finding the court did not have jurisdiction to consider the claim, Mr. Justice
Cavanagh held at para. 70 that the plaintiff’s claim would require the
Court to review matters within the Legislative Assembly’s exclusive
jurisdiction “over its own proceedings and its decision making in respect of
appointment or reappointment of a parliamentary officer whose role relates to
the Assembly’s work in holding government to account”. Cavanagh J. continued at
paras. 71–73:

[71]      The Plaintiff submits that because
he is not seeking a right of reinstatement, a successful claim would not impair
the work of the Assembly or any of its members. The Plaintiff submits that, if
he is successful, his only entitlement would be to damages and the Assembly’s
concerns will not materialize, I disagree. An adjudication of the Plaintiffs
claim would require the court to hear evidence concerning the conduct of the
Assembly in relation to its motives and its internal process leading to the
decision not to reappoint the Plaintiff to the office of Ombudsman. The
Plaintiffs claim for damages, if it were to proceed to adjudication, would
still require the Assembly to be subject to an external review by the court of
a matter within its exclusive jurisdiction.

[72]      I conclude that this action puts
into issue the internal process and procedures of the Assembly
in relation
to the appointment of a parliamentary officer
, the Ombudsman of Ontario,
who fulfills part of the Assembly’s role in holding the government to account.
I
agree with the Assembly that a trial of this action would require the court to
inquire into the manner in which the Assembly exercised recognized and
constitutionally-guaranteed categories of parliamentary privilege that are
within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Assembly. These categories are with
respect to (i) the Assembly’s own internal proceedings, including development
and delivery of an address of the Assembly, and (ii) the Assembly’s hiring of,
management: of and decision not to reappoint a parliamentary officer whose role
relates to the Assembly’s work in holding government to account for the conduct
of the province’s business.

[73]      Therefore, this court does not
have jurisdiction to adjudicate this action against the Assembly.

[Emphasis added.]

[
49
]

Like
the ombudsperson
in
Marin
, the Legislative Assembly contends that the
RCY is a statutorily appointed role with a statutory remuneration scheme. The
Legislative Assembly argues that to make inquiries about this role would engage
its internal proceedings and management of the plaintiff as RCY.

[
50
]

The Legislative Assembly also points to
March
v. Hodder,

2007 NLTD 93
[
March
], where the plaintiff brought an
application to quash a resolution of the House of Assembly of Newfoundland and
Labrador, on procedural fairness grounds, that called for his removal for cause
as the statutorily-appointed Citizens’ Representative. In dismissing the claim,
Mr. Justice Orsborn found that, even with the procedural fairness issues
raised by Mr. March, an inquiry into the House’s workings would be
improper and would significantly impair its dignity and efficiency: at paras. 64–66.

[
51
]

The Legislative Assembly points specifically to para. 68
of
March
in which Orsborn J. linked the decision to make the Citizens’
Representative an officer of the House with the conclusion that his removal was
central to its functioning. The Legislative Assembly contends that as in
March
,

if this Court were to inquire into the plaintiff’s entitlement to
remuneration outside the statutory scheme, its ability to carry out its
deliberate and legislative functions would be impaired.

[
52
]

The plaintiff contends that this case is
distinguishable from both
Marin

and
March
. In those cases, the plaintiff’s
claims would have required the court to inquire into the legislature’s choices
concerning appointment and removal. She contends that the present case does not
involve such an inquiry. Indeed, the plaintiff argues that adjudicating the
claims in this case would not require the court to delve into the Legislative
Assembly’s legislative or deliberate choices or impair the Legislative Assembly
in any way. In essence, the plaintiff is asking the court to consider a private
law claim.

[
53
]

As the plaintiff points out, there is no blanket
privilege over all the legislature’s relations with all employees:
Vaid

at
para.
75
. This was most recently affirmed by Karakatsanis J. in
Chagnon

at para.
36
.
At para. 37 she made the following comments:

The present case highlights the difficulty
with trying to recognize a category of privilege that includes
all aspects
of the management of a
group of employees and decisions with regards to
all
functions these employees
perform (see E. Fox-Decent, "Parliamentary Privilege, Rule of Law and the
Charter after the Vaid Case" (2007), 30:3
Can. Parl. Rev.
27, at p. 31).
The requirements of the necessity test may be more easily fulfilled where the
scope of autonomy that is claimed pertains to control and oversight over
certain functions performed by some parliamentary employees, or certain aspects
of their employment relationship. That said, the parties have not framed this
case in that way. The President asserts a parliamentary privilege over the
management of the security guards as a category of employees. This privilege
would immunize not only their dismissals, but all of their employment
conditions (from salary to seniority) from review on any grounds.

[
54
]

Although the defendants dispute that the
plaintiff was an “employee”,
Vaid
and
Chagnon
make clear that the
legislature does not have blanket immunity over all aspects of managing its
staff. While
Marin
held that there was a category of privilege over
proceedings and decision-making in respect of appointment or reappointment, I
am not satisfied that the plaintiff’s claims, which are fundamentally concerned
with contractual entitlement to remuneration and benefits as a result of
appointment, are within an established category of privilege.

[
55
]

I am also not prepared to accept that the
reasoning in
March

applies in this case. Despite dealing with the
termination of a legislative officer, the Court in
March

was focussed on
the
activity
(debating and passing resolutions) not the
subject
matter
(managing or terminating of legislative officers) as deserving
immunity: see paras. 63–64. The sphere of activity in question in
March
,
debating and passing resolutions, is clearly at the core of the legislative and
deliberative function of the legislature and is distinguishable from the case
at bar.

[
56
]

Ultimately, the adjudication of the plaintiff’s
claims will not require the court to inquire into the manner in which the Legislative
Assembly exercised, recognized and constitutionally-guaranteed categories of
parliamentary privilege.

[
57
]

I turn now to whether the Legislative Assembly
has discharged its burden to demonstrate that
sphere of activity in the plaintiff’s
claim is
“so closely and directly
connected with the fulfilment by the assembly or its members of their functions
as a legislative and deliberative body . . . that outside interference would
undermine the level of autonomy required to enable the assembly and its members
to do their work with dignity and efficiency”
:
Chagnon

at para. 43,
Vaid

at para. 46.

[
58
]

The Legislative Assembly argues that legislative
officers’ remuneration is “thoroughly entwined” with the discharge of statutory
duties and any interference with the remuneration scheme would undermine the
Legislative Assembly’s autonomy required to conduct its business.

[
59
]

The plaintiff argues that parliamentary
privilege should not apply to immunize
legislatures from claims in private
law.

[
60
]

I
n
Roberts v. Commissioner of the NWT
,
2002 NWTSC
68
,
Ms. Roberts’ appointment as the Conflict of
Interest Commissioner for the Northwest Territories was revoked. Mr. Justice
Vertes accepted that legislative assemblies may enter into contractual
relationships with their officers and that enforcement of those contracts would
fall to the courts.

At para. 56 Vertes J. concluded that the legislature in that case chose to
make an otherwise privileged conduct subject to judicial scrutiny by
statutorily fixing a term of appointment and entering into a contract: at para. 55.

[
61
]

At para. 63 Vertes J. held that:

63        Actions taken by the Assembly with
respect to the Conflict Commissioner's tenure affect her contractual rights.
These actions are related to a contractual relationship, not to some functioning
of the legislative process. Breaching a contract could not, to employ the terms
used in
Vaid
[FCA] (
supra
), fall within the rules by which the Legislative
Assembly conducts its business. As noted by Campbell J. in
Thompson v.
McLean

(1997),
1998 CanLII 14740 (ON CTGD)
,
37
C.C.E.L. (2d) 170
(Ont. Ct. Gen. Div.), at 177-178:

Parliamentary
privilege is not an end in itself, but simply a means to ensure that the
legislature has whatever protection it needs in order to go about its
parliamentary business without being second guessed by the courts.

The courts, while
vigilant to ensure that they do not interfere with the business of the
legislature, must also be vigilant to ensure that parliamentary privilege is
not carried so far that it interferes unnecessarily with the right of citizens
to have access to the courts in relation to matters that do not interfere with
the parliamentary business of the legislature. As Hugessen A.C.J. said in
R.
v. Atlantic Sugar Refineries Col

(1976),
1976 CanLII 1254 (QC CS)
,
67
D.L.R. (3d) 73
(Que. S.C.) at p. 87:

Absolute privilege
is a drastic denial of the right of every citizen who believes himself wronged
to have access to the Courts for redress and should not be lightly or easily
extended.

[
62
]

As a
result, the plaintiff contends that when the Legislative Assembly chose to
contract outside the
RCY Act
, enforcement of those contractual claims
and representations made in the negotiations that preceded them may properly
fall to the courts.

[
63
]

The
plaintiff also argues that immunizing the government from review of its
contractual obligations would be inappropriate, particularly in this case. The
RCY’s independence, rather than supporting immunity, suggests that contractual
remuneration must be reviewable because financial security is a core characteristic
of independence:
Wells

v. Newfoundland
,
1999 CanLII 657 (SCC)
, [1999] 3 S.C.R. 199
at para.
44
. The plaintiff contends that holding the
legislature to account with what it promised her and preventing it from
reneging on that promise, helps ensure the legislature

and its members can proceed fearlessly and without interference to fulfil their
individual and collective roles.

[
64
]

In this case, t
he Legislative Assembly
clearly had the authority to appoint an RCY under the provisions of the
RCY
Act
. I accept that it was a fundamental objective of the
RCY Act

to
ensure that the RCY was independent from government and it was with that
objective that the plaintiff was appointed by the Legislative Assembly as the
RCY, an officer of the legislature, subject to statutory term limits, and
reported as such to the Legislative Assembly.

[
65
]

While, like the Ombudsman in

Marin
,
the
RCY is a statutorily appointed role, with remuneration in respect of salary,
pension benefits, and expense reimbursement, prescribed and limited by the
RCY
Act
, allowing the plaintiff’s contractual claim go to trial will not require
the court to inquire into the Legislative Assembly’s internal proceedings. Nor
will the claim require an inquiry into the Legislative Assembly’s management of
the plaintiff as RCY. The adjudication of the plaintiff’s claims will also not
require the hearing of evidence concerning the conduct of the Legislative Assembly
in relation to its motives and its internal process leading to the decision to appoint
the plaintiff to the office of the RCY like in
March
.

[
66
]

The Legislative Assembly did not explain exactly
how judicial scrutiny of whether it has fulfilled contractual terms regarding
remuneration and benefits would interfere with its legislative and deliberative
functions, offend its dignity, or violate the separation of powers. As in
Vaid

and
Chagnon
,

the defendants here have not demonstrated that
an inquiry into the plaintiff’s claim is so closely and directly connected with
Legislative Assembly’s fulfillment of its legislative and deliberate functions that
judicial interference would undermine its ability to do its work.

[
67
]

I find that the parliamentary privilege asserted
in this case is cast too broadly. The privilege to which the Legislative Assembly
is entitled is the right to regulate its internal affairs, proceedings, and the
plaintiff’s appointment, but its scope does not preclude the enforcement of the
plaintiff’s contractual rights to the compensation she was entitled to receive
for her role once appointed, nor her claim for damages if she was induced into
accepting an appointment as the RCY by the negligent representations of those
permitted to discuss her compensation with her.

[
68
]

The plaintiff’s claim does not impugn any acts
of the Legislative Assembly that are sufficiently connected to its core
legislative and deliberative functions such that a court’s review of those acts
would interfere with its work. I conclude that inquiring into and ensuring that
the contracts the Legislative Assembly chooses to enter into are not within
parliamentary privilege.

[
69
]

As the Legislative Assembly’s application to
strike the plaintiff’s amended notice rests entirely on the doctrine of
parliamentary privilege, the Legislative Assembly’s application is dismissed in
its entirety. The Government’s application is dismissed to the extent it relies
on parliamentary privilege.

B.        Does
the Plaintiff’s Amended Notice Disclose a Reasonable Claim?

[
70
]

To succeed under this ground, the Government
must demonstrate that it is “plain and obvious, assuming the facts pleaded to
be true, that the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action”:
Imperial
Tobacco
at para. 17;
Moses

at para.
41
.

[
71
]

The Government argues that, as a matter of law,
the plaintiff has no claim against it on four grounds.

[
72
]

First, it says that the alleged verbal contract
is clearly unenforceable as it is contrary to the
RCY Act
. The
Government asserts that the plaintiff’s “salary, benefits and pension
entitlements were prescribed and limited by the
RCY Act
”. Pursuant to
s. 3(2) of the
RCY Act
and
s. 1(1)
of the
Public Sector
Pension Plans Act
, S.B.C. 1999, c. 44, the RCY’s pension entitlement is
limited to no more than 12 months for each year of service
.
The Government
argues that, as a result, the
RCY Act
did not permit the pension
entitlement that the plaintiff says was agreed to and therefore, the alleged
agreement is unenforceable and the claim against it must fail.

[
73
]

In support of this position, the Government
referred me to the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in
Wells
,
which it says stands for the proposition that a contractual term which
contravenes an express statutory limitation is unenforceable. In
Wells
,
the
plaintiff had been appointed and was statutorily entitled to hold office until
the age of 70 with good behaviour. Approximately six years from his pension
vesting, a new statute was passed that abolished his position. Mr. Justice
Major, for a unanimous Court, held at page 213 that:

[T]he employment relationship remains a
contract in substance and the general law of contract will apply unless
superseded by explicit terms in the statute or agreement.

[
74
]

Accordingly, the defendant argues that the plaintiff’s
claim in contract must be struck as it is contrary to the express wording of
the
RCY Act
.

[
75
]

In my view,
Wells
does not assist the Government.
While a statute may supersede an agreement by express language, the mere
existence of a statute does not necessarily mean that a party cannot contract outside
the statutory wording. At page 218, Major J. held that:

In the absence of a clear express intent to
abrogate rights and obligations – rights of the highest importance to the
individual – those rights remain in force. To argue the opposite is to say that
the government is bound only by its whim, not its word. In Canada this is
unacceptable, and does not accord with the nation’s understanding of the
relationship between the state and its citizens.

[
76
]

In
Wells
, Major J. also held at para. 18:

The respondent's entitlement to compensation
hinges on the nature of his relationship with the Crown. If he had a contract
of employment with the Crown, then his termination will constitute a breach
compensable in damages. If, on the other hand, his relationship was purely
statutory, then he is limited to administrative remedies.

[
77
]

At para. 48, Major J. explained:

The principled restriction on the Crown's
ability to breach contractual obligations without consequence was endorsed by
Professor P. W. Hogg, in
Liability of the Crown
(2nd ed. 1989), at
pp. 171-72, where he wrote:

I acknowledge the possibility that, on rare
occasions, the Crown may feel compelled by considerations of public policy to
break a contractual undertaking. If there were no doctrines of executive
necessity, the ordinary law of contract would apply, and would require the
Crown to negotiate with the other party for a variation or release, or to pay
damages for its breach of contract. That is surely the right result. It
provides compensation for the injured contractor. It requires the public purse
to bear the cost of the change of public policy.

It is conceivable that a case might arise
where the government cannot accept the decision of a court holding the Crown
liable for breach of contract. For example, a court might award damages that
were so high as to place an intolerable cost on a desired public policy. The
solution to this case is legislation. The Parliament or Legislature has the
power to cancel a contract, and this power is not limited by any obligation to
pay compensation. Similarly, judicial decisions can be retroactively reversed
or modified. The Canadian Charter of Rights does not provide any general
protection for private property or any general prohibition on retroactive laws.
Through legislation, therefore, the will of the community can be made to
prevail over private contract rights. That is the ultimate safeguard of public
policy.

[
78
]

Importantly, at para. 55, Major J.
concluded that:

The Crown had a contractual obligation to
the respondent, which it breached by eliminating his position. As his right to
seek damages for that breach was not taken from him by legislation, he is
entitled to compensation.

[
79
]

Legislation may, by express language, preclude a
claim or prevent a plaintiff from seeking a remedy, but the legislation in this
case does not do so. There is no language that expressly removes the
plaintiff’s right to seek damages for breach of contract or tort. While it
provides for the RCY’s remuneration, there is also no language that precludes
additional remuneration or benefits on top of those provided by statute. As the
plaintiff points out, for example, some benefits, such as vacation days, were
not addressed in the
RCY Act
even though the plaintiff was permitted 40
days of annual paid vacation for which she negotiated. I find that the
legislation does not proscribe that those entitlements could not be
supplemented by agreement.

[
80
]

Furthermore, the mere fact that the
RCY Act

did not permit the pension entitlement she claims does not mean her claim is
bound to fail. The plaintiff deposed that the Deputy Clerk informed her that,
following considerable review of her pension requirements by various
individuals including the Attorney General, approval had been given for her
pension formula to be amended such that she would receive 1.5 years of pension
entitlement for each year of service.

[
81
]

While it may be that an amendment to the
RCY
Act
with respect to pension entitlement

was sought but refused,
there is no evidence before me to that effect. Even if such an amendment was
sought and refused, that may be no answer to the plaintiff’s claim for
negligent misrepresentation. Whether the verbal agreement alleged by the
plaintiff would have been effected by legislation (such as amending her
statutory entitlements) or other administrative means, does not necessarily
make it unenforceable. The plaintiff contends that she would not have agreed to
accept an appointment as RCY for only the remuneration set out in the
RCY
Act
. The question remains as to whether the parties agreed to supplement
the plaintiff’s statutory entitlements by contract to persuade her to accept
the appointment.

[
82
]

Ultimately, I am unable to conclude that the
language of the
RCY Act
overrides the contract alleged by the plaintiff
such that it is plain and obvious that she has no reasonable claim.

[
83
]

Second, the Government contends that the
Legislative Assembly is the only proper party against which the plaintiff may
bring her claim. The Government argues that the Legislative Assembly is the
“decision maker” who is statutorily empowered to appoint, suspend or remove the
RCY under
ss. 2(1)
,
4(2)
, and
4(3)
of the
RCY Act
. Indeed, the
entire purpose of the
RCY Act
was to create a position that would be
independent from the Government. The Government argues that it and the
plaintiff were not in a relationship of appointer and appointee, nor were any
of the indicia of employment present.

[
84
]

The Government further points out that the RCY
is an officer of the Legislative Assembly, not the government. Relying on
Marin

and
Roberts
, it contends that as an officer of the legislature, the
plaintiff has no claim against it because her legal rights can be only be
asserted against the Legislative Assembly.

[
85
]

I am not prepared to accept the plaintiff’s
submission on these applications that the fact that she was enrolled in the Government’s
employment benefits program and pension program, or that her “employer” listed
on her T-4 document is the Government is determinative of an employment
relationship with the Government. It is unnecessary for me to resolve that
contention in order to deal with the applications before me, and I will
therefore leave that issue to be resolved, if necessary, on the trial of the
plaintiff’s claims.

[
86
]

In this case, the Government concedes that due
to the unique fact that the plaintiff was the first RCY, there was a necessary
transition from the
OCY Act
to the
RCY Act
, and a similar
transition from the CYO to the RCY. As a result, the plaintiff entered into two
written agreements whereby she was the CYO from January 1, 2007 until March 31,
2007, as agreed to by the Attorney General, and RCY beginning in November 2006
for a five year term. Because of these agreements, I find that the plaintiff’s
claim that she had, in part, a contractual relationship with the Government is
a reasonable one, and I decline to dismiss it on the basis that it is not. I
find, as well, that it is reasonable for the plaintiff to attempt to establish
what she was told the terms of that contractual relationship would be. The fact
that the Legislative Assembly was the party who appointed her does not
necessarily mean that the Government cannot be liable if it made
representations to her in this context.

[
87
]

Third, the Government argues that as a matter of
law, it cannot be vicariously liable for representations made by the Deputy
Clerk who was a permanent officer of the Legislative Assembly. In support of
this argument, the Government points to the separate appointment powers
provided in ss. 4 and 39 of the
Constitution Act
and that the
Deputy Clerk was appointed to the Legislative Assembly under s. 39.

[
88
]

Even though there are separate appointment
powers under the
Constitution Act
, the Government has not provided any
legal reason why the Deputy Clerk could not negotiate on its behalf or act as
agent for both it and the Legislative Assembly when he was dealing with the
plaintiff on matters that concerned both defendants. Further, the plaintiff’s
evidence is that the Attorney General, Deputy Attorney General, and other
provincial government employees participated in the process of negotiating and
finalizing her contractual entitlements. The Government tendered no contrary
evidence. Therefore, I am unable to conclude that the pleadings, taking as
true, disclose no reasonable claim on this basis.

[
89
]

Fourth and finally, the Government argues that
it cannot be liable as a “common employer” to the plaintiff. The Government says
that its role as “paymaster” and the fact that the plaintiff was registered in
its employment benefits and pension program, does not make it a common employer
of an officer of the Legislative Assembly. The Government contends that the
plaintiff was paid a salary consistent with the
RCY Act
, which also
provides that the Government will be “paymaster”, a role which it describes as
“perfunctory”.

[
90
]

The Government points to the fact that the
Legislative Assembly funds the RCY’s office annually by approving an
appropriation from the consolidated revenue fund that results in the annual
Supply
Act
, which includes the annual salary, benefits, and out-of-pocket expenses
for the RCY. It argues that this fact does not make it the plaintiff’s
employer.

[
91
]

Further, the Government argues that an officer
of the legislature is not an employee and the Legislative Assembly has the sole
jurisdiction over all aspects of her appointment. The Government says that
applying the common employer doctrine would be contrary to separation of powers
principles and the legislative scheme of the
RCY Act

as it dictates that
the Legislative Assembly has sole jurisdiction over the appointment of the RCY.

[
92
]

Based on the submissions and the pleadings, I am
unable to conclude that the plaintiff’s claim should be struck on this basis. The
Supreme Court has continually affirmed that courts should refrain from striking
claims that are novel but arguable. While the Government has emphasized the
separation of powers, that is not enough to discharge its burden of
demonstrating that the plaintiff’s claim discloses no genuine legal or factual
basis.

[
93
]

Therefore, I decline to strike any aspect of the
plaintiff’s claims under Rule 9-5(1)(a).

C.        Is the Plaintiff’s Claim Unnecessary or Frivolous?

[
94
]

I turn now to whether the plaintiff’s claim is
“unnecessary” or “frivolous”, whether it does not go to establishing a cause of
action or does not advance a claim known in law:
Woolsey

at para.
28
.
This ground of the applications was brought pursuant to
Rules
9-5(1)(b) which
does not preclude evidence to support it.

[
95
]

The Government says that the written agreements
provide a complete answer to the plaintiff’s claim: the only remuneration and
benefits the plaintiff would receive as CYO were those provided in her position
as RCY. It says that the plaintiff’s allegation that she continued to do work
as CYO past March 30, 2007—when her term of appointment came to an end—is
“untenable”. At this point, the Government argues, the position of CYO ceased
to exist and her government appointment came to an end, with no further compensation
owed to her.

[
96
]

There is no dispute that the Attorney General
appointed the plaintiff as CYO. The plaintiff and the Government agreed that
her only compensation for that role was the entitlements she was owed as the RCY.
While the Legislative Assembly appointed the plaintiff as RCY, and the Attorney
General appointed her as CYO, there was one, not two, sets of negotiations for
the remuneration and benefits that the plaintiff would receive for both
positions. The plaintiff was paid one package of benefits for her work as both
RCY and CYO. Therefore, her compensation as CYO was intimately tied to that as
RCY.

[
97
]

In the result, I am unable to find that the
plaintiff’s claim against the Government is unnecessary or frivolous.

D.        Does
the Plaintiff’s Amended Notice Disclose a Genuine Legal or Factual Issue for Trial?

[
98
]

The Government contends that the plaintiff’s
claim against it should be dismissed pursuant to Rule 9-6(4) on the basis that there
is no genuine legal or factual issue for trial.

[
99
]

The Government contends that the written agreements
are conclusive evidence that the plaintiff has no reasonable prospect of
success with her contractual claim against it.

[
100
]

These agreements were respectively between the Government,
represented by the then Attorney General, and the plaintiff, confirmed by
letter dated December 13, 2006, and between the Chair of the Child and Youth
Transition team, on behalf of the same Attorney General, and the plaintiff,
confirmed by letter dated March 27, 2007. Each of these letters were signed and
accepted by the plaintiff confirming that she was the CYO from January 1, 2007
until March 31, 2007. Each stated, “… your only remuneration for the term of
your acting appointment will be your salary and benefits as the Representative
for Children and Youth.”

[
101
]

The plaintiff has admitted the authenticity of these written agreements
but she contends that she was verbally promised additional remuneration and
benefits if she accepted the appointment. The plaintiff’s evidence was that the
Attorney General assured her that the Government would meet her compensation
needs and that he approved the pension element of her remuneration. Clearly she
did not receive what she says she was promised.

[
102
]

The plaintiff further asserts that her responsibilities as CYO
continued well past March 30, 2007. She contends that the transitional
provisions in the
RCY Act
fail to capture all of the work the plaintiff
performed after March 30, 2007, in relation to her CYO appointment leaving open
the question of whether all of the work she performed as CYO after March 30,
2007 was performed pursuant to those transitional provisions.

[
103
]

On this application, the Government did not adduce any evidence to dispute
the alleged verbal agreement or the representations that the plaintiff alleges
were made to her. Importantly, on this application the Government does not
assert that the verbal agreement and misrepresentations alleged by the
plaintiff were not made, nor does it seek to establish by evidence that the
Deputy Clerk did not bind it to pay the plaintiff under the alleged verbal agreement.

[
104
]

I am unable to accept that the wording of the written agreements necessarily
overcomes the plaintiff’s claim for either breach of contract or negligent
misrepresentation.

[
105
]

The pleadings contain sufficient material facts to support her
claims and present a genuine legal or factual issue for trial.

VI.       CONCLUSION

[
106
]

The applications by the Government and the Legislative Assembly are
dismissed.

“The Honourable Chief Justice Hinkson”
